wars.name: Cantabrian and Asturian Wars
wars.outcome: Roman victory; final conquest of the Iberian peninsula, mass deportation of hill populations to the plains, foundation of Asturica Augusta and Lucus Augusti; gold mines of the north-west opened
wars.summary: The last war of conquest in Spain, fought in the Cantabrian mountains and Asturias by up to seven or eight legions. Augustus campaigned in person in 26 BC but fell ill; the decisive work was done by his legates, ending with Agrippa's brutal pacification in 19 BC.
wars.detail: Statilius Taurus and Calvisius Sabinus had campaigned against the Cantabri and Vaccaei from 29 BC, but the main war began in 26 BC when Augustus took personal command from a base at Segisama, using a three-pronged advance supported by a fleet from Aquitania landing on the Cantabrian coast. After victories at Vellica and the blockade of Aracillum, Augustus retired sick to Tarraco and closed the doors of Janus in 25 BC, prematurely. Publius Carisius and Gaius Antistius continued against the Astures (Lancia) and the Cantabri; revolts followed in 24, 22 and 19 BC. Agrippa ended resistance in 19 BC after his own troops had become demoralised, disgracing legio I (which lost the title Augusta) for cowardice. Survivors of military age were massacred or forced down to the plains. The war secured the gold districts of Las Médulas and the north-west, which by Pliny's day produced 20,000 lb of gold a year. The legions IV Macedonica, VI Victrix and X Gemina remained in the north for decades; Florus and Orosius, both dependent on Livy's lost books, are the main narrative sources, supplemented by archaeology of Roman siege camps at sites such as La Loma and El Cincho.

phases.t: Preliminary campaigns of Statilius Taurus and Calvisius Sabinus
Augustus's personal campaign; Vellica, Aracillum, Lancia
Recurrent risings suppressed by Lucius Aemilius, Gaius Furnius and Publius Carisius

wars.name: Roman-Kushite War
wars.outcome: Negotiated peace at Samos (21/20 BC): Augustus remits the tribute, Rome keeps the Dodekaschoinos with a frontier at Hiera Sykaminos
wars.summary: Kushite forces under the one-eyed 'Candace' (probably queen Amanirenas) and prince Akinidad took Syene, Elephantine and Philae while the Egyptian garrison was weakened by Aelius Gallus's Arabian expedition. The prefect Gaius Petronius drove them back, sacked Napata and garrisoned Primis, but Augustus settled on generous terms.
wars.detail: The Kushites carried off statues of Augustus; the bronze head of Augustus found buried under the steps of a victory temple at Meroë (now in the British Museum) is almost certainly one of them, placed so that visitors trod on it. Petronius counterattacked with fewer than 10,000 infantry and 800 horse, defeated a large army at Pselchis, took Primis (Qasr Ibrim) and razed Napata, then retired, leaving 400 men and two years' supplies at Primis. When the Candace attacked Primis in 22 BC Petronius relieved it. Kushite envoys, sent on to Augustus at Samos, obtained the cancellation of the tribute Petronius had imposed. Strabo, a friend of Aelius Gallus, gives the Roman version; Meroitic inscriptions (the Hamadab stelae of Amanirenas and Akinidad) are still only partly understood. The frontier then remained stable for nearly three centuries.

phases.t: Second Kushite attack on Primis; peace of Samos

wars.name: Augustan Alpine Wars
wars.outcome: Roman conquest of the entire Alpine arc; creation of Raetia, Noricum and the Alpine prefectures; Tropaeum Alpium lists 45 subdued peoples
wars.summary: A series of operations that secured the Alpine passes between Italy and the Rhine-Danube: the destruction of the Salassi in 25 BC, the annexation of Noricum c. 16-15 BC, and the double pincer of Drusus and Tiberius against the Raeti and Vindelici in 15 BC, followed by the reduction of the Maritime Alps in 14 BC.
wars.detail: In 15 BC Drusus advanced from Italy up the Adige and over the Brenner or Reschen pass while Tiberius came from Gaul, fought a naval action on Lake Constance and met his brother near the sources of the Danube; the campaign ended, by tradition, on 1 August, a date Horace celebrated (Odes 4.14). Large parts of the male population were deported. The trophy at La Turbie (7/6 BC) named 45 gentes Alpinae devictae; Pliny copied the text (NH 3.136-137) and fragments survive. The Cottian kingdom of Marcus Julius Cottius was left as a client prefecture (arch at Susa, 9/8 BC).

phases.t: Noricum incorporated; Raeti and Vindelici conquered
Ligurian peoples of the Maritime Alps subdued

wars.name: Bellum Pannonicum (Pannonian War of Tiberius)
wars.outcome: Roman control extended to the Drava and the middle Danube; Illyricum enlarged; Tiberius awarded ovatio (9 BC)
wars.summary: After Agrippa's death in 12 BC Tiberius took over the war in Pannonia, using the Scordisci as allies, and subdued the Breuci and other peoples between the Sava and the Drava, deporting the young men. Velleius and Dio give only outlines.
wars.detail: Agrippa's arrival in winter 13/12 BC had frightened the Pannonians into submission; his death led them to revolt. Tiberius campaigned in 12-9 BC; Augustus's Res Gestae (30) claims that Pannonian peoples never reached by a Roman army before were subdued and the frontier of Illyricum advanced to the Danube. The disarmament and levies imposed in these years were a key grievance behind the great revolt of AD 6. The Senate voted Tiberius a triumph, which Augustus commuted to an ovatio.

wars.name: Augustan Germanic Wars
wars.outcome: Rome abandons the attempt to create a province between Rhine and Elbe after Varus's defeat (AD 9) and Germanicus's recall (16); the Rhine becomes the frontier
wars.summary: Twenty-eight years of campaigning east of the Rhine, from Drusus's offensives of 12-9 BC to Germanicus's last expedition in AD 16. By AD 9 a province was being organised, with towns such as Waldgirmes; the loss of three legions in the Teutoburg region reversed this.
wars.detail: The war began as retaliation for the clades Lolliana (16 BC) but became a war of conquest: Drusus reached the Elbe in 9 BC, Tiberius deported 40,000 Sugambri in 8 BC, Domitius Ahenobarbus crossed the Elbe and built the pontes longi, and Tiberius's immensum bellum of AD 4-5 brought a fleet up the Elbe. The planned pincer against Maroboduus in AD 6 was aborted by the Pannonian revolt. Excavations at Waldgirmes (forum with a gilded equestrian statue of Augustus), Haltern, Anreppen, Hedemünden and Kalkriese show a province in formation, which ancient writers (Dio 56.18) also describe. After AD 9 Germanicus's three campaigns (14-16) avenged Varus and recovered two eagles but at great cost in men and ships; Tiberius recalled him, preferring to leave the Germans to their internal quarrels, and Arminius fought Maroboduus in 17. The eagle of legio XIX was recovered in 15, another in 16 and the third in 41.

phases.t: Tiberius's immensum bellum; fleet on the Elbe
Tiberius and Germanicus secure the Rhine

wars.name: Great Illyrian Revolt (Bellum Batonianum)
wars.outcome: Revolt crushed; Illyricum split into Pannonia and Dalmatia; but Rome's capacity to conquer Germany is fatally weakened
wars.summary: The most dangerous rising Rome faced under Augustus. Triggered by levies for the Marcomannic war, the Daesitiates under Bato and the Breuci under another Bato and Pinnes rose in AD 6. Suetonius calls it the gravest foreign war since the Punic Wars; at its height Tiberius commanded ten legions, 70 auxiliary cohorts and 14 alae.
wars.detail: Velleius, who served in it, claims 800,000 rebels with 200,000 infantry and 9,000 cavalry under arms, and that Augustus warned the Senate the enemy could reach Rome in ten days. Augustus resorted to a levy of freedmen (the first since Cannae). Tiberius's strategy was attritional: wasting the countryside, dividing the rebel zones, and refusing pitched battle; it drew criticism in Rome and Germanicus was sent with a second army. The Breucian Bato betrayed Pinnes and was executed by the Daesitiate Bato, who in turn surrendered at Andetrium in 9 after Germanicus took Raetinium, Splonum and Arduba. Asked why he had rebelled, Bato said 'You Romans are to blame, for you send as guardians of your flocks not dogs or shepherds but wolves' (Dio 56.16). News of the victory reached Rome five days before news of Varus's disaster.

phases.t: Battle of the Volcaean Marshes; Germanicus arrives
Surrender of the Breuci at the Bathinus river
Reduction of the Dalmatian strongholds; Bato surrenders

wars.name: War of Tacfarinas
wars.outcome: Tacfarinas killed at Auzea in 24 by Publius Cornelius Dolabella; Roman control of the Numidian steppe consolidated
wars.summary: A seven-year guerrilla war in Africa led by Tacfarinas, a Numidian deserter from Roman auxiliary service who drilled the Musulamii and their Moorish allies in Roman fashion. Three governors won triumphal ornaments without ending it.
wars.detail: Furius Camillus defeated Tacfarinas in 17; Lucius Apronius in 20 decimated a cohort that had fled (a rare imperial instance) and saw a veteran, Helvius Rufus, win the civic crown at Thala; Junius Blaesus in 22-23 broke his bands into small columns and blockhouses and was the last non-imperial general hailed as imperator. Legio IX Hispana was brought from Pannonia as reinforcement and withdrawn too early. Tacfarinas's demand for land, delivered by envoys to Tiberius, enraged the emperor (Tac. Ann. 3.73). Dolabella finally surprised him at Auzea, where he died fighting; the Senate refused Dolabella triumphal ornaments to avoid embarrassing Blaesus, Sejanus's uncle.

wars.name: Roman conquest of Britain
wars.outcome: Southern and central Britain become a province; Wales subdued by 78; northern Britain overrun by Agricola to Mons Graupius (83/84) but abandoned north of the Forth-Clyde line within a few years
wars.summary: Begun by Claudius in 43 with four legions under Aulus Plautius and continued by a series of governors over four decades, the conquest of Britain was Rome's largest territorial gain of the first century and a test-bed for client kingship (Togidubnus, Prasutagus, Cartimandua).
wars.detail: Claudius needed military glory; the pretext was the flight of Verica of the Atrebates. After the Medway and the fall of Camulodunum, the legions fanned out: II Augusta under Vespasian to the south-west, IX Hispana north towards Lincoln, XIV Gemina and XX into the Midlands. Ostorius Scapula disarmed the allies (provoking an Icenian revolt in 47), founded the veteran colony at Camulodunum (49) and defeated Caratacus (51). The Silures defied Rome for decades. Suetonius Paullinus's attack on the Druid centre of Mona was interrupted by Boudica's revolt (60/61). The Flavians resumed the advance: Petillius Cerialis against the Brigantes (71-74), Julius Frontinus in Wales (74-77), Agricola from 77 to 84 into Caledonia. Tacitus's Agricola, written by the governor's son-in-law, is the main narrative and is panegyric; Vindolanda tablets and the excavated fortress of Inchtuthil, abandoned unfinished c. 86-87, illustrate the withdrawal that followed when troops were needed on the Danube.

phases.t: Didius Gallus, Veranius, Suetonius Paullinus; Mona and Boudica
Cerialis and Frontinus: Brigantes and Silures

wars.name: Boudican Revolt
wars.outcome: Revolt crushed at the battle of 'Watling Street'; Boudica dies; Iceni lands ravaged; Paullinus recalled after a critical report by the freedman Polyclitus
wars.summary: Rising of the Iceni and Trinovantes under Boudica after the annexation of the Icenian kingdom, the flogging of the queen and rape of her daughters, and the exactions of the veterans of Camulodunum and of Seneca's loans. The rebels destroyed Camulodunum, Londinium and Verulamium before being defeated by Suetonius Paullinus.
wars.detail: Tacitus gives 70,000 citizens and allies killed in the three towns and 80,000 Britons killed in the final battle against 400 Romans; Dio adds lurid detail of atrocities and a speech for Boudica with a hare released for divination. The date is 60 in Tacitus (Annals) but 61 is often preferred from the sequence of governors. Burnt destruction horizons of the period are well attested in Colchester and London. The procurator Decianus Catus fled to Gaul; the camp prefect of legio II Augusta, Poenius Postumus, refused to march and afterwards fell on his sword. Nero reportedly considered abandoning Britain (Suet. Nero 18).

phases.t: Outbreak while Paullinus attacks Mona; Camulodunum, Londinium, Verulamium destroyed
Battle and reprisals; Classicianus and Polyclitus

wars.name: Roman-Parthian War over Armenia (58-63)
wars.outcome: Compromise of Rhandeia: the Arsacid Tiridates keeps Armenia but receives the diadem from Nero in Rome (66)
wars.summary: Nero's war over Armenia, fought by Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo, who took Artaxata (58) and Tigranocerta (59) and installed Tigranes VI. After Tigranes provoked Parthia, Caesennius Paetus was humiliated at Rhandeia (62); Corbulo then negotiated the settlement that held for half a century.
wars.detail: Corbulo spent 55-57 restoring the discipline of the Syrian legions (Tacitus describes soldiers who had never seen a camp or done sentry duty) and wintered them in the Armenian highlands under canvas. His campaigns combined manoeuvre with exemplary brutality. The Rhandeia formula, a Parthian prince as king of Armenia crowned by Rome, became the template for Roman-Parthian relations until Trajan. Tacitus's account is pro-Corbulo, probably drawing on the general's own memoirs.

wars.name: First Jewish-Roman War
wars.outcome: Destruction of Jerusalem and the Second Temple (70); end of the high priesthood and Sanhedrin in their old form; legio X Fretensis garrisons Jerusalem; fiscus Judaicus imposed on all Jews
wars.summary: The great revolt of Judaea, which began in 66 with the cessation of sacrifices for the emperor and the defeat of Cestius Gallus at Beth Horon. Vespasian reconquered Galilee and the countryside in 67-68; Titus besieged and destroyed Jerusalem in 70; the last fortresses, Herodium, Machaerus and Masada, fell by 73 or 74.
wars.detail: Causes included procuratorial misrule (Gessius Florus's seizure of 17 talents from the Temple treasury), Greek-Jewish strife at Caesarea, social banditry and apocalyptic expectation. Josephus, a rebel general in Galilee who surrendered at Jotapata and predicted Vespasian's accession, wrote the Jewish War under Flavian patronage, first in Aramaic, then Greek; it is the fullest account of any Roman provincial war but is apologetic both for the Flavians and for the Jewish aristocracy, blaming the 'brigands' and Zealots. Rebel coins (silver shekels 'Jerusalem the holy', bronze 'for the freedom of Zion') give the insurgents' own voice. The war gave the Flavians their legitimating victory, commemorated on the Arch of Titus, the Temple of Peace and IUDAEA CAPTA coinage.

phases.t: Perea, Judaea and Idumaea; operations pause for the civil war

wars.name: Civil War of the Year of the Four Emperors
wars.outcome: Vespasian emerges as emperor, founding the Flavian dynasty; Lex de imperio Vespasiani
wars.summary: The civil wars that followed Nero's fall: Vindex's rising and defeat (68), Galba's brief reign and murder (Jan 69), Otho's defeat at the first battle of Bedriacum (Apr 69), and the Flavian victory over Vitellius at the second battle (Oct 69) and in Rome (Dec 69). Tacitus: 'the secret of empire was out, that an emperor could be made elsewhere than at Rome'.
wars.detail: Each phase was decided by provincial armies: the Rhine legions for Vitellius, the Danube legions (led by the charismatic Antonius Primus, acting ahead of Vespasian's strategy) and the eastern legions for Vespasian. Mucianus marched the Syrian army west; Vespasian held Egypt and the grain supply. Cremona was sacked for four days; the Capitol burned. Tacitus's Histories 1-3 (our main source, closely parallel with Plutarch's Galba and Otho, implying a common lost source, perhaps Pliny the Elder or Cluvius Rufus) dramatise the moral collapse of the soldiery.

phases.t: Otho vs Vitellius; Flavian rising; Bedriacum II; sack of Rome

wars.name: Batavian Revolt
wars.outcome: Revolt ended by negotiation after defeats by Petillius Cerialis; Batavi keep their privileges; four legions dissolved or reconstituted
wars.summary: Julius Civilis, a Batavian noble and Roman citizen, rose ostensibly for Vespasian against Vitellius in 69 but turned it into a war of independence; Batavian veteran cohorts, Germanic tribes and the 'Empire of the Gauls' joined. The Rhine legions at Vetera surrendered and were massacred, and others swore allegiance to the Gallic empire, the worst humiliation of Roman arms in the first century.
wars.detail: Tacitus portrays Civilis as a one-eyed Sertorius or Hannibal who dyed his hair red and vowed not to cut it until he destroyed the legions. The Bructeran seeress Veleda received the captured legate Munius Lupercus (who died en route) and a captured flagship. Cerialis arrived in spring 70 with legions from Italy, Spain and Britain, won at Rigodulum and at Trier, survived a night attack, and defeated Civilis in a two-day battle near Vetera. Tacitus's narrative breaks off mid-negotiation (Hist. 5.26). Legiones I Germanica, IV Macedonica, XV Primigenia and XVI Gallica were disbanded; IV Flavia and XVI Flavia were raised in their place.

phases.t: Surrender of Vetera; Imperium Galliarum; Cerialis's counteroffensive

wars.name: Domitian's Chattan War
wars.outcome: Roman annexation of the Taunus and Wetterau; road network and watchtowers that grow into the upper German limes; Domitian takes the title Germanicus
wars.summary: Domitian's own campaign against the Chatti, launched from Mogontiacum in 83 under the pretext of a census in Gaul. Tacitus mocked his triumph as a sham with slaves dressed as captives, but archaeology shows real territorial gains and the cutting of 120 Roman miles of frontier roads (limites).
wars.detail: Frontinus, who served on the campaign, describes how Domitian cut limites through forests to expose the Chatti's hiding places (Strategemata 1.3.10) and paid compensation for crops destroyed by forts (2.11.7). Germania Superior and Inferior were formally constituted as provinces around this time (by 90). Coins of 85 proclaim GERMANIA CAPTA. Tacitus (Agr. 39; Germ. 37) and Pliny (Pan. 16) are hostile.

phases.t: Fortification of the Taunus and Wetterau

wars.name: Domitian's Dacian War
wars.outcome: Compromise peace of 89: Decebalus a client king receiving Roman subsidies and engineers
wars.summary: Dacian raids across the Danube killed the governor of Moesia, Oppius Sabinus, in winter 85/86. Domitian came in person; his praetorian prefect Cornelius Fuscus invaded Dacia and was killed with much of his army; Tettius Julianus avenged him at Tapae in 88, but the revolt of Saturninus and trouble with the Marcomanni forced a negotiated peace.
wars.detail: Moesia was split into Superior and Inferior in 86. The peace terms (Dio 67.7) granted Decebalus money and artisans 'skilled in all the arts of peace and war', which Trajan later represented as shameful tribute; Diegis, Decebalus's brother, received a diadem from Domitian. Domitian celebrated a triumph de Dacis in 89. Whether a legion (often supposed V Alaudae) was destroyed with Fuscus is debated. The Tropaeum Traiani's companion altar at Adamclisi may commemorate the fallen of 86 rather than of 102, an unresolved debate.

wars.name: Domitian's Suebic and Sarmatian Wars
wars.outcome: Sarmatians defeated by 93 (Domitian's ovatio, laurel only); fighting with the Suebi continues into 97 when Nerva takes the title Germanicus
wars.summary: The Marcomanni and Quadi refused aid against Dacia and were attacked in 89; in 92 the Iazyges with Suebic allies destroyed legio XXI Rapax. Domitian took the field himself in Pannonia (92-93).
wars.detail: A poorly documented war that set the pattern for the Marcomannic Wars of the 160s. The loss of XXI Rapax is inferred from Suetonius (Dom. 6) mentioning a legion slaughtered with its legate, combined with the legion's disappearance. Pannonia's garrison was raised to four legions in these years, shifting the empire's military centre of gravity to the middle Danube.

phases.t: Punitive campaign against Marcomanni and Quadi
Iazyges invasion; XXI Rapax destroyed; Domitian in Pannonia

wars.name: First Dacian War
wars.outcome: Decebalus submits: surrenders arms, engineers and deserters, demolishes forts, cedes territory (Banat, Oltenia); Roman garrison at Sarmizegetusa
wars.summary: Trajan's first war against Decebalus, launched in March 101 with perhaps nine legions and as many auxiliaries. After a costly victory at Tapae, a Dacian and Roxolanian counterattack into Moesia in winter 101/102, and a converging advance on the Orăștie mountains, Decebalus sued for peace.
wars.detail: Trajan's Column (scenes I-LXXVIII) is the principal visual source, but it is an artistic composition, not a war diary; Trajan's own commentarii (Dacica) survive in a single phrase quoted by Priscian. Dio (via the Byzantine epitome of Xiphilinus) provides the narrative skeleton, including a message written on a giant mushroom by the Buri. Trajan accepted the title Dacicus and triumphed in late 102. Decebalus was allowed to keep his throne as client.

phases.t: Crossing at Lederata; advance on Tapae
Dacian-Roxolanian raid on Moesia; battle near Adamclisi
Assault on the Orăștie mountain fortresses; peace

wars.name: Second Dacian War
wars.outcome: Dacian kingdom destroyed; Decebalus's suicide; province of Dacia created; vast booty
wars.summary: Decebalus rearmed, attacked Roman garrisons, captured the commander Longinus and tried to assassinate Trajan. Trajan crossed by his new stone bridge at Drobeta, besieged Sarmizegetusa Regia in summer 106 and hunted down the king, whose head was displayed on the Gemonian stairs.
wars.detail: John Lydus, citing Trajan's doctor Criton, gives booty of 5 million pounds of gold and 10 million of silver, figures modern scholars (Carcopino's 'gold of the Dacians') have tried to rationalise, perhaps by dividing by ten. Decebalus's treasure had been buried under the diverted river Sargetia and was betrayed by a noble named Bicilis. Longinus took poison to prevent his use as a bargaining chip. The province was colonised with settlers 'from the whole Roman world' (Eutropius 8.6), a claim later fuelling the Daco-Roman continuity debate.

phases.t: Siege of Sarmizegetusa; death of Decebalus; annexation

wars.name: Trajan's Parthian War
wars.outcome: Armenia, Mesopotamia and Assyria briefly annexed, Ctesiphon taken and a client king installed; massive revolts and the Jewish diaspora rising force retreat; Hadrian abandons the conquests in 117
wars.summary: Provoked by Osroes I's deposition of the Armenian king Axidares, Trajan annexed Armenia in 114, conquered northern Mesopotamia in 115 and marched down the Euphrates to Ctesiphon and the Persian Gulf in 116. Revolts across the new provinces and a failed siege of Hatra ended the enterprise.
wars.detail: Trajan refused the submission of Parthamasiris at Elegeia, who was then killed under murky circumstances. Dio has him weeping at Charax that he was too old to follow Alexander to India. Lusius Quietus and Erucius Clarus retook Nisibis, Edessa and Seleucia in 116; Maximus Santra was killed. Trajan crowned Parthamaspates king at Ctesiphon, effectively admitting he could not hold Babylonia. Ancient and modern judgements diverge: Lepper and others see a rational frontier strategy for controlling Mesopotamian trade; others (Bennett) stress glory-seeking. Hadrian's withdrawal was represented by hostile tradition as envy.

wars.name: Diaspora Revolt (Kitos War)
wars.outcome: Jewish communities of Cyrenaica, Egypt and Cyprus destroyed or reduced to insignificance; Jews banned from Cyprus
wars.summary: Simultaneous Jewish uprisings in Cyrenaica, Egypt, Cyprus and Mesopotamia while Trajan was campaigning in Parthia. Dio claims 220,000 killed in Cyrene and 240,000 in Cyprus; papyri and inscriptions confirm widespread devastation in Egypt and Cyrene.
wars.detail: Led in Cyrene by Lukuas/Andreas, the rebels destroyed temples of Apollo, Zeus and Hecate and the Caesareum and baths at Cyrene, as inscriptions recording Hadrianic restoration show. In Egypt the strategos Apollonios of Apollinopolis Heptakomias appears in his family letters fighting the 'impious Jews'; the great synagogue of Alexandria was destroyed. Marcius Turbo was sent with land and sea forces; in Mesopotamia Lusius Quietus crushed the Jewish population, the name surviving in rabbinic 'Polemos shel Qitos'. The causes (messianism, Greek-Jewish hostility, fiscus Judaicus) are debated; the sources (Dio's epitome, Eusebius, Orosius, papyri) are fragmentary.

phases.t: Mesopotamia; suppression by Turbo and Quietus

wars.name: Bar Kokhba Revolt
wars.outcome: Revolt crushed with enormous loss of life; Jerusalem refounded as Aelia Capitolina and closed to Jews; Judaea renamed Syria Palaestina
wars.summary: The second great Jewish revolt, led by Simon bar Kosiba, hailed by Rabbi Akiva as 'Bar Kokhba' (son of the star). Rome had to bring Sextus Julius Severus from Britain and units from across the empire; Hadrian omitted the customary 'I and the army are well' from his letter to the Senate.
wars.detail: Dio (69.12-14) gives 50 fortresses and 985 villages destroyed and 580,000 killed in battle, besides those who died of hunger and disease. Causes cited are the foundation of Aelia Capitolina (Dio) and a ban on circumcision (HA Hadr. 14.2); the relative priority is disputed, as is whether the rebels ever held Jerusalem. The Nahal Hever and Wadi Murabba'at caves have yielded letters from Bar Kosiba himself (in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek), the Babatha archive and land leases dated by the 'redemption of Israel'. Legio XXII Deiotariana may have been destroyed in the revolt, though evidence is circumstantial. Hadrian took a second imperatorial acclamation; the commanders received triumphal ornaments.

phases.t: Outbreak; rebels control Judaean hill country
Julius Severus's war of attrition; fall of Betar
Mopping up in the Judaean desert caves

wars.name: Roman-Parthian War of Lucius Verus
wars.outcome: Roman victory: Armenia restored to a Roman client, Osroene and Dura-Europos under Roman control, Seleucia and Ctesiphon sacked; but returning troops spread the Antonine Plague
wars.summary: Vologases IV invaded Armenia in 161, destroyed a Roman army at Elegeia and defeated the governor of Syria. Lucius Verus was sent east; his generals Statius Priscus, Avidius Cassius and Martius Verus won the war while Verus stayed mostly at Antioch and Daphne.
wars.detail: Priscus took Artaxata in 163 and founded a new Armenian capital, Kaine Polis; Sohaemus, a Roman senator of Arsacid-Emesene descent, was installed as king. Cassius advanced down the Euphrates, won at Dura and Sura, and in 165 sacked Seleucia on the Tigris despite its submission, and burned the palace at Ctesiphon. In 166 he crossed into Media. Lucian's satirical 'How to Write History' mocks the flood of sycophantic histories of this war; Fronto's letters and Principia Historiae offer the court view.

wars.name: Marcomannic Wars
wars.outcome: Rome restores the Danube frontier after near-catastrophe; Marcus's plans for provinces of Marcomannia and Sarmatia abandoned by Commodus in the peace of 180
wars.summary: A generation of war along the middle Danube, beginning with an incursion of Langobardi and Obii in 166/167 and culminating in the first barbarian invasion of Italy for nearly three centuries, when Marcomanni and Quadi besieged Aquileia and destroyed Opitergium. Marcus Aurelius spent most of his last decade at Carnuntum, Sirmium and Vindobona, writing the Meditations.
wars.detail: The war is divided into the first (bellum Germanicum, 166/167-175) and second (expeditio Germanica secunda, 177-180) phases, separated by the revolt of Avidius Cassius. Rome faced a coalition of Marcomanni, Quadi, Iazyges and many smaller peoples, partly pushed by movements further north (the Goths moving towards the Black Sea). The Antonine Plague crippled recruitment; Marcus enrolled slaves, gladiators and bandits and auctioned palace treasures in 169. Captured Germans were settled inside the empire, a precedent for later centuries. The chronology is highly uncertain because Dio survives only in excerpts and the Historia Augusta is muddled; the Column of Marcus, coin legends, and inscriptions such as Laugaricio and the career of Valerius Maximianus provide anchors. Whether Marcus intended to annex Marcomannia and Sarmatia (HA Marc. 24.5, 27.10) is debated.

phases.t: Incursions; Marcus and Verus go north
Failed Roman offensive; invasion of Italy; Costoboci raid Greece
Campaigns against Marcomanni, Quadi, Iazyges; Rain Miracle
Second expedition; Roman garrisons in Quadi lands; death of Marcus
